en: Paraśurāmakalpasūtra 1. Section: The Ritual of Initiation (Dīkṣāvidhi).
Now, therefore, we shall explain initiation. Parks_1.1.

The Blessed One, the venerable Paramaśiva, having effortlessly composed all eighteen branches of knowledge beginning with the Vedas as well as all philosophical systems (*darśana*) by assuming their respective forms, was questioned by the Goddess Bhairavī—who consists of pure consciousness and is non-different from his own self—and he then composed the five *Āmnāyas*, which constitute the essence of the ultimate reality, through his five faces. (Parks 1.2)
In this regard, the established tenet is as follows: // Parks_1.3 //
The universe consists of thirty-six principles. (Parks 1.4)
Śiva encased in the body is the individual soul (jīva); Śiva free from the body is the Supreme Śiva (paraśiva).
Self-reflection is the goal of human endeavor.
Words consist of phonemes and are eternal. (Parks 1.7)
The inconceivable power of mantras.
Through both the oral tradition and faith, all accomplishments are attained. (Parks 1.9)
Validity consists primarily in trustworthiness. (Parks 1.10)
Through the friction of the oneness of the guru, the mantra, the deity, the self, the mind, and the vital breath, there arises the realization of the inner self.
Bliss is the form of Brahman,
and that is established within the body;
its manifestors are the five makāras.
By them, worship is performed in secret; through public display, there is hell.
Through the firmness of cultivation, the perfection of mastery is attained. (Parks 1.13)
Not disparaging any philosophical system. // Parks_1.14 //
The non-counting of anything whatsoever.
The disclosure of secrets [is permitted] only to a worthy disciple. (Parks 1.16)
Always maintaining the application of knowledge. // Parks_1.17 //
The constant immersion in the state of Śiva. // Parks_1.18 //
The avoidance of desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, envy, as well as unrighteous violence, theft, and anything loathed by the world. // Parks_1.19 //
Devotion to a single guru is beyond doubt. (1.20)
In all things, there is the state of being without possession.
Performing action while having abandoned its fruit. // Parks_1.22 //
The neglect of impermanent duties. // Parks_1.23 //
Even when the fivefold sequence is not obtained, there is a retrospective reflection upon the perpetual sequence.
Fearlessness in all circumstances. // Parks_1.25 //
All that is to be known is the oblation; the senses are the sacrificial ladles; the powers are the flames; one's own self is Śiva, the purifier; and he himself is the priest. (Parks 1.26)
The fruit is the discernment of consciousness that is free from objects.
There is nothing superior to the attainment of self.
This is the established style of the treatise. (Parks 1.29)
Like courtesans, the sciences such as the Vedas are manifest;
this science, however, is hidden within all philosophical systems. (Parks 1.30)
In that regard, a wise person should undergo initiation in every respect. // Parks_1.31 //

There are three initiations: the Śāktī, the Śāmbhavī, and the Māntrī. Among these, the Śāktī [is so called] because of the entry of power (śakti), the Śāmbhavī because of the placement of the feet, and the Māntrī because of the instruction of mantras; one should perform all of them. (Parks 1.32)
Some say that it is one by one. (Parks 1.33)

The true guru, having set in motion the ritual sequence and performed the oblation together with its ancillaries, being filled with youthful exuberance, calls the disciple and binds his face with a cloth; having sprinkled him with drops from the vessels of Gaṇapati, Lalitā, Śyāmā, Vārtālī, and Parā, he causes him to hear the established doctrine.
Having visualized a red and white foot upon his head, one should adorn his entire body, which has been washed with that nectar. // Parks_1.35 //

Having meditated upon that surging wave of light, blazing like a flaming fire, extending from the soles of his feet up to the vault of Brahma, and having burned away his bonds of sin with its rays; // Parks_1.36 //

Having worshipped with the six-limbed mantra of Bālā a new pitcher filled with water scented with *trikaṭu*, *triphalā*, *caturjāta*, *takkola*, *madayantī*, *sahadevī*, *dūrvā*, ashes, clay, sandalwood, saffron, and *rocanā*, along with camphor, and wrapped in a pair of cloths; having placed therein the wheels (*cakra*) of Śrī, Śyāmā, and Vārtālī,
and having worshipped them with the mantras of the three enclosures (*āvaraṇa*), one should protect it with the *astra* mantra and display the *dhenu* and *yoni* mudrās.

Having seated the disciple within the Mātṛkā-yantra— a golden pericarp joined with Śiva, possessing eight filaments endowed with pairs of vowels, having eight petals joined with the eight groups of letters beginning with *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, *ya*, and *śa*, situated in the eight directions, and with *ṭhaṃ* and *vaṃ* in the square— he should bathe him with the water from that jar using the three Vidyās.

Having seated the disciple— who was dressed in fine silk, anointed with unguents, adorned with ornaments, and wearing a turban— beside him, and having projected the *mātṛkā* onto his body; then, having placed three first-portion flower-segments, sprinkled with sandalwood water and freed from their cloth wrappings, into the hand of that disciple, and having made him consume them with the *tattva-mantras*, he instructed the boy in his right ear, and thereafter...
One should recite the desired mantra. (Parks 1.39)

Then, having placed his own foot upon the disciple's head and having taught him all the mantras— either all at once or in sequence according to his capacity— and having touched some part of his own body against a part of the disciple's body, he should bestow upon him a name consisting of two, three, or four syllables beginning with the *mātṛkā* letters of that specific limb and ending with the word "Ānandanātha. (Parks 1.40)
Before instructing the child, one should first give them one's own sandals inscribed with the six-syllable mantra.
Having instructed him in the rules of conduct,

having touched his heart-consciousness, and having wiped that limb three times with the threefold knowledge and embraced him, he should smell him on the crown of the head and make him one with his own self-nature. // Parks_1.42 //

The disciple, too, having meditated upon fullness and accomplished his purpose, should honor that guru with wealth according to his capacity; thus, having known what is to be known, he becomes authorized in all mantras—may there be auspiciousness!
Chapter 2: The Manual on Gaṇanāyaka.
Having thus received initiation from a true guru, one should study the manual of Gaṇanāyaka in order to remove obstacles to the propitiation of Mahāvidyā.

Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, with his entire body bathed by the flowing stream of nectar-drops trickling from the pair of feet of the Guru seated in the center of the pericarp of the thousand-petaled lotus at the *dvādaśānta*, he should meditate— while restraining the movement of his breath and mind— upon the multi-faced [deity] blazing in the center of the heart-lotus, as red as a rising sun and serving as the expiation for all defects; then, his body turned pale-red by the mass of that radiance, having gone outside and discharged his excrement and urine, [he should proceed].

Having performed the cleansing of the teeth, bathing, putting on of garments, and the offering of water (arghya) to the Sun, [one should worship] Mahāgaṇapati, who dwells in the rising sun, with the mantra:
“We know that Tatpuruṣa; we meditate upon Vakratuṇḍa.”
"May that Dantī inspire us. Having thus offered the *arghya* and performed the daily duties (*nityakṛtya*), one should perform the fourfold libation (*caturāvṛttitarpaṇa*).
Longevity, health, sovereignty, strength, nourishment, great fame, poetic talent, enjoyment, and liberation—these result from the fourfold libation. (Parks 2.2)

First, having offered libations twelve times with the root mantra, one should offer libations four times each to the twenty-eight syllables of the mantra ending in *svāhā*, and likewise offer libations four times to the root mantra; then again, [one should offer to] the thirteen pairs consisting of Śrī and Śrīpati, Girijā and Girijāpati, Rati and Ratipati, Mahī and Mahīpati, Mahālakṣmī and Mahālakṣmīpati, Ṛddhi and Āmoda, Samṛddhi and Pramoda, Kānti and Sumukha, Madanāvatī and Durmukha, Madadravā and Vighnadrāviṇī, Vighnakartṛ and Vasudhārā, Śaṅkhanidhi and Vasumatī, and Padmanidhi.
One should satisfy each individual deity four times and the root mantra four times;
thus, there are four hundred and forty-four acts of satisfaction (*tarpaṇa*). // Parks_2.3 //

Now, as for the ritual procedure for sacrifice: having returned home and smeared the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*), one should worship at the doorway on both sides with "Salutation to Bhadrakālī" and "to Bhairava," and above the door with "Salutation to Lambodara. Having entered within and sat upon the seat with the *āsana-mantra*, one should restrain the breath (*prāṇāyāma*), perform the placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga-vinyāsa*), and effect a pervasive distribution (*vyāpaka*) using the root mantra. Then, one should contemplate the Deity within oneself, with his side embraced by Siddhalakṣmī.

Having meditated upon Vighneśvara, who has the crescent moon as his crest-ornament, whose complexion is reddish-pink, whose eleven hands are adorned with a citron, a mace, a *puṇḍra* flower, a sugarcane bow, a trident, the *sudarśana* discus, a conch, a noose, a blue lotus, a cluster of grain, the tip of his own tusk, a jewel-jar, and a water-pot; who has a flowing ichor from his temples, who is full of bliss, and who is the destroyer of all obstacles—(one should worship him). Parks 2.4.

In front [of oneself], having fashioned a triangle, a hexagon, a circle, and a square with pure water consecrated seven times with the root mantra and worshipped with perfumes, unbroken rice, and flowers, and having scattered flowers therein; then, having performed the placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) in the southeast, northeast, southwest, northwest, the center, and the cardinal directions, [one should offer] with the mantra:
"Obeisance to the support of the arghya vessel, which is the fire-maṇḍala consisting of ten kalās; obeisance to the sun-maṇḍala consisting of twelve kalās."

Having filled the arghya vessel with pure water while reciting, "Salutation to the arghya vessel; salutation to the lunar orb, whose self consists of sixteen digits; salutation to the nectar of the arghya," one should protect it with the Astra-mantra, conceal it with the Kavaca-mantra, and display the cow and yoni mudrās. (Parks 2.5)

Having consecrated it seven times and sprinkled oneself and the ritual implements with droplets of that water, one should fashion the previously mentioned mandala with that water, join the first [syllable] in the same manner, and having placed the second and middle [syllables] there, one should worship the digits of Fire, Sun, and Moon with the *Vakratuṇḍa-gāyatrī* and with this verse: "Obeisance to you, O Gaṇeśa... (*gaṇānāṃ tvā*).

Having consecrated [the water] with mantras and performed protection with the *astra* and other [mantras], one should worship the Guru’s sandals on the head three times with drops of that [water]. // Parks_2.6 //
In front, upon a seat fashioned from red sandalwood, or on an image of Mahāgaṇapati, or on a wheel consisting of a square, an eight-petaled lotus, a hexagon, and a triangle,
[one should worship] Tīvrā, Jvālinī, Nandā, Bhogadā, Kāmarūpiṇī, Ugrā, Tejovatī, Satyā,
and Vighnanāśinī; and [the syllables] *ṛṃ* for Dharma, *ṝṃ* for Jñāna, *ḷṃ* for Vairāgya, *ḹṃ* for Aiśvarya, *ṛṃ* for Adharma, and *ṝṃ*.

Having worshipped the pedestal-energies (*pīṭhaśakti*) with "Obeisance to Ignorance (*ajñāna*), ḶṂ; Obeisance to Non-detachment (*avairāgya*), ḸṂ; Obeisance to Non-sovereignty (*anaiśvarya*"), and having worshipped the group of eight beginning with Dharma, one should utter the root mantra and invoke Mahāgaṇapati with the words "I invoke Mahāgaṇapati. Having performed the fivefold worship (*pañcopacāra*) and satisfied him tenfold, one should perform the worship of the five enclosures (*pañcāvaraṇa*) consisting of the couples, the limbs, Brāhmī and the others, and Indra and the other [deities] by means of the root mantra. (Parks 2.7)
In the triangle is the Deity; within that hexagon are the four couples beginning with Śrī and Śrīpati, as well as the limbs (aṅgas); in the hexagon are the six couples beginning with Ṛddhi and Āmoda;

on both sides of the hexagon are two couples, and at its joints are the limbs; in the eight petals are Brāhmī and the others, and in the eight directions of the square are Indra and the others—all these should be worshipped by prefixing the name of each deity with "Śrī" and pronouncing the word "pādukā."
One should join the eight-syllable mantra: "I worship. (Parks 2.8)
Having thus worshipped the five obstacles (pañcāvaraṇī) and again propitiated the deity Gaṇanātha tenfold, having served him with the sixteen types of offerings (ṣoḍaśopacāra),
and having recited three times "Oṃ Āḥ, to all obstructing spirits and all elemental beings, hūṃ svāhā," and having offered the sacrificial oblation (bali),
one should summon one Baṭuka with the thought that he is Gaṇapati, and one Śakti with the thought that she is Siddhalakṣmī, [honoring them] with perfumes, flowers, and consecrated rice (akṣata).

Having worshipped the beginning, the end, and the middle, and having caused [the deities] to grant their favor by saying, "May the accomplishment of my mantra be free from obstacles," one should pay homage and recite [the mantra] according to one's capacity. // Parks_2.9 //

If the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) is to be performed, one should first offer oblations according to the rules into the consecrated fire with mantras beginning with "Śrī" and "Śrīpati" and ending with the "Vighnakartṛs," each followed by *svāhā*. Having returned and gratified the Deity three times, and having accepted the fivefold expansion (*pañcaka*) together with those who are fit, one should dissolve the Great Gaṇapati into oneself; thus, with one's resolve accomplished, one may dwell in happiness—may there be auspiciousness! (Parks 2.10)
3. Section: Śrīkrama.

Having thus worshipped Gaṇapati and thereby dispelled the entire web of obstacles, one should commence the ritual sequence (krama) of the venerable Lalitā, the sole sovereign of the wheel of energies (śakticakra). // Parks_3.1 //
At the hour of Brahmā, having abandoned sleep, a Brahmin should contemplate the Guru, who is the form of Supreme Śiva, for the dissolution of his sins. (Parks 3.2)

Having meditated upon the blazing root-consciousness, which extends from the base to the aperture at the crown of the head, tawny like millions of lightning flashes and as yellowish-red as the rising sun, and having thereby destroyed the web of defilements with its rays, one should mentally repeat the root mantra—beginning with *ka* or *ha*—ten times. (Parks 3.3)

When the time for the ritual bath has arrived, having offered three handfuls of water with the *mūla-mantra*, having drunk water consecrated by that mantra three times, having performed the libation (*tarpaṇa*) three times, and having sprinkled oneself three times, one puts on two garments, utters "hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ saḥ," and offers an *arghya* three times to Savitṛ, saying: "To Mārtāṇḍabhairava, together with the Śakti Prakāśā, svāhā. (Parks 3.4)

Having meditated upon the wheel of nine sources (navayonicakra) in the center of that mandala, having uttered the mantra: "We know Tripurasundarī" (*tripurasundari vidmahe*), having uttered "Kāma," then "we meditate on Pīṭhakāminī" (*pīṭhakāmini dhīmahi*), and having uttered "Śakti," [one says] "may She, the Wet One, impel us" (*tan naḥ klinnā pracodayāt*).

Having thus offered arghya three times to the Great Goddess, having touched [the vessel] one hundred and eight times while reciting the mantra, and having observed silence, [one should proceed]. (Parks 3.5)
Having gone to the sacrificial hall, either adorned with ornaments or free from the desire for such adornment, he sat down upon his seat with the seat-mantra.
Having recited the *tritārī*, one should cast a handful of flowers upon the ground, saying: "Homage to Dīpanātha, who is joined with twelve red śaktis. (Parks 3.7)
At the beginning of all mantras, there is the conjunction of the three stars (tritārī);
the three stars are Vāk, Māyā, and Kamalā. (Parks 3.8)

In front of him, having placed the great king of mandalas—which consists of the union of the five Śaktis and four Śrīkaṇṭhas; which is composed of the earth-pavilion, the three lines, the earth-leaves, the directional leaves, the worlds, the spokes, the Brahmā-spokes, the sun-spokes, the corners, the intermediate corners, the triangle, and the bindu; and which is either drawn with vermilion and saffron or engraved in gold, silver, the five metals, jewels, crystal, and so forth—[he should proceed].

There, in that great wheel, for the ocean of nectar, for the island of jewels, for the magnificent grove of various trees, for the garden of *kalpavṛkṣa* trees, for the garden of *santāna* trees, for the garden of yellow sandalwood, for the garden of *mandārava* flowers, for the garden of *pārijāta* trees, for the garden of *kadamba* trees,
for the wall of *puṣparāga* gems, for the wall of *padmarāga* gems, for the wall of *gomedha* gems, and for the wall of *vajra* gems.
To the wall of lapis lazuli jewels, to the wall of sapphire jewels, to the wall of pearl jewels, to the wall of emerald jewels,
to the wall of coral jewels, to the pavilion of rubies, to the pavilion of a thousand pillars, to the pool of nectar, to the pool of bliss,
to the pool of discernment, to the exhalation of morning sunlight, to the exhalation of moonlight, to the great rampart of erotic grace, and to the forest of great lotuses.

To the king of palaces made of wish-fulfilling gems; to the eastern gate consisting of the Eastern Tradition (Pūrvāmnāya); to the southern gate consisting of the Southern Tradition (Dakṣiṇāmnāya); to the western gate consisting of the Western Tradition (Paścimāmnāya); to the northern gate consisting of the Northern Tradition (Uttarāmnāya);
to the circle of jewel-lamps; to the great lion-throne made of jewels; to the single foot of the dais consisting of Brahmā; to the single foot of the dais consisting of Viṣṇu;
to the single foot of the dais consisting of Rudra; to the single foot of the dais consisting of Īśvara; to the single plank of the dais consisting of Sadāśiva; to the couch with swan-down pillows.

Having meditated upon and worshipped each of those [objects] with the forty-four mantras beginning with "Homage to the great pillow of swan-down, to the saffron-colored coverlet, to the great canopy, and to the great curtain," [he performed the ritual]. Parks 3.10.

Having offered perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice grains, and so forth on the right side, and having placed lamps all around, one should worship the wheel with the root mantra in the first triangle using the three sections of the root mantra.
Having performed the drying, burning, and flooding [of the body] through breath-control (prāṇāyāma) associated with the colors of wind, fire, and water, [one should proceed]. // Parks_3.12 //
Having restrained the breaths three times. (Parks 3.13)
"May those beings depart who dwell upon the earth;
may those beings who create obstacles perish by the command of Śiva!

Having spoken thus, striking the ground with the heel of his left foot, clapping his hands, and raising his face upward, he should give three *tāla* slaps and, endowed with the sense of identity with the Goddess (*devy-ahambhāva*), perform the array of the vajra-armour (*vajrakavaca*) upon his own body.
Having performed the purification of the hands by means of Śrīkaṇṭha, Ananta, and Tārtīya, joined with the *bindu*, from the middle finger down to the palms. // Parks_3.15 //
Having uttered the *kumāri* mantra and the words "Mahātripurasundarī," one should place the palms together in *añjali* at the heart, saying, "Protect me, protect me! (Parks 3.16).

Having recited the *māyā*, *kāma*, and *śakti* [bījas], and having offered his own seat with the mantra "Homage to the seat of the Goddess's self" (*devyātmāsanāya namaḥ*), [he should proceed]. (Parks 3.17)
Having recited *śiva-yuga-bālām* [HŪṂ HŪṂ HRĪṂ], one says *śrīcakrāsanāya namaḥ*; having recited *śiva-bhṛgu-yuga-bālām* [SA HA SA HA HRĪṂ], one says *sarvamantrāsanāya namaḥ*;

and having recited *bhuvana-madanau blem* [HRĪṂ KLĪṂ BLEM], one says *sādhyasiddhāsanāya namaḥ*. Thus, having established the seat for the mantra-deity of the wheel within the wheel by means of these three mantras. (Parks 3.18)
By turning away from the fool, he has established the six limbs through the placement of fingers numbering three, two, one, ten, three, and two.
Having pronounced the vowels together with their *bindus* as *blūm*, [one says] "Salutation to Vaśinī Vāgdevatā" on the head.
In all cases, there is the addition of the *bindu* to the consonant groups (*vargas*).
Having uttered the *ka*-group and *kalahrīṃ*, [one says] "Salutation to Kāmeśvarī Vāgdevatā" on the forehead.
Having uttered *cuṃ* and *ga*, one should say *nvlīṃ modinīvāgdevatāyai namaḥ* at the center of the eyebrows;
having uttered *ṭuṃ* and *bha*, one should say *ylūṃ vimalāvāgdevatāyai namaḥ* at the throat; and having uttered *tuṃ* and *ca*, one should say *jmrīṃ aruṇāvāgdevatāyai namaḥ* at the heart.
Having uttered *puṃ* and *hslvyūṃ*, one should say "Salutation to the speech-deity Jayinī" at the navel;
having uttered the four letters beginning with *yā* and *jhmryūṃ*, one should say "Salutation to the speech-deity Sarveśvarī" at the generative organ;
and having pronounced the six letters beginning with *śā* and *kṣmrīṃ*, one should say "Salutation to the speech-deity Kaulinī" at the base. (Parks 3.20)

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the fifteen syllables of the root-mantra upon the crown of the head, the base, the heart, the three eyes, the two ears, the mouth, the pair of arms, the back, the pair of knees, and the navel— either by placing them in the sixfold wheel (*ṣoḍhā-cakra*) or otherwise.

Having drawn a mandala consisting of a triangle, a hexagon, a circle, and a square on the left side with pure water, having worshipped it with flowers, having established a conch vessel with its stand, having filled it with pure water, having added the initial drop (*ādimabindu*), and having worshipped it with the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), one should consecrate it with the Vidyā; then, sprinkling oneself and the articles of worship with droplets of that water. // Parks_3.22 //

Having prepared a maṇḍala consisting of a triangle, a hexagon, a circle, and a square with that water, one should worship the center with the Vidyā, the triangle with the sections of the Vidyā, and the hexagon with the surrounding seed-syllables. Then, uttering the word "vāc," one should install the support for the arghya vessel with the mantra: "Obeisance to the support of the arghya vessel, which is the Agni-maṇḍala, the self of ten kalās. Having worshipped the support, one should worship the fire-born kalās.

Having prepared [the vessel] with the mantra, "Obeisance to the solar disc above Madana, consisting of twelve kalās, the arghya-vessel," and touching the vessel, he should fill it with the solar kalās using the mantra, "Sauḥ! Obeisance to the lunar disc, consisting of sixteen kalās, the nectar of the arghya. Then, having offered the first [kalā], he should worship the second and the middle [eighth] of the sixteen kalās of the moon.

There, having drawn a triangle with its sides beginning with the letters *a*, *ka*, and *tha*, shining with a swan (*haṃsa*) situated at the end of the pair of lines *ha* and *la*, with its corners joined by *vāc*, *kāma*, and *śakti*; having worshipped it with the *haṃsa* mantra and constructed a circle outside the six-cornered figure; having worshipped the six-cornered figure starting from the front side with the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*);
having consecrated it seven times with the root mantra; and having offered perfume, unbroken rice, flowers, incense, and lamps, he sprinkled the articles of worship with those droplets.
Having made everything consist of knowledge (vidyā), one should touch it and recite the ninety-four mantras. // Parks_3.25 //
The thirty-eight digits of the threefold fire (*tejastritaya*) are conjoined with the three *tārās* (the *praṇava*, *hrīṃ*, and *strīṃ*).
The ten digits of Brahmā are: Sṛṣṭi, Ṛddhi, Smṛti, Medhā, Kānti, Lakṣmī, Dyuti, Sthira, Sthiti, and Siddhi.
The ten digits of Viṣṇu are: Jarā, Pālinī, Śānti, Īśvarī, Rati, Kāmikā, Varadā, Āhlādinī, Prīti, and Dīrghā.
Tīkṣṇā, Raudrī, Bhayā, Nidrā, Tandrī, Kṣudhā, Krodhinī, Kriyā, Udgarī, and Mṛtyu are the ten Rudra-kalās.
Pītā, Śvetā, Aruṇā, and Asitā are the four Īśvara-kalās.
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, Śānti, Indhikā, Dīpikā, Recikā, Mocikā, Parā, Sūkṣmā, Amṛtā, Jñānā, Ajñānā, Amṛtāpyāyinī, Vyāpinī, and Vyomarūpā are the sixteen Sadāśiva-kalās.

The swan dwelling in purity, the Vasu dwelling in the mid-air, the Hotṛ-priest dwelling on the altar, the guest dwelling in the house; dwelling among men, dwelling in the best places, dwelling in Truth, dwelling in the sky; born of the waters, born of the kine, born of Truth, born of the mountains—the Great Truth.
For that heroic deed Viṣṇu is praised, like a fearsome beast, roaming and dwelling in the mountains;
in whose three wide strides all the worlds abide.
We worship Tryambaka, the fragrant, the increaser of prosperity.
May I be liberated from death, as a cucumber from its stem, yet not be separated from immortality.
The wise ever behold that supreme abode of Viṣṇu,
like an eye extended in the sky.
The wise, ever-vigilant, and inspired singers kindle that which is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
May Viṣṇu prepare the womb; may Tvaṣṭṛ fashion the forms;
may Prajāpati pour [the seed]; may Dhātṛ place the embryo within you.
Bestow a fetus, O Sinīvālī; bestow a fetus, O Sarasvatī.
May the two divine Aśvins, adorned with lotus-garlands, place a fetus within you.
Thus, these are the five mantras.
And including the root-vidyā, there are ninety-four mantras in total.
Now, some indeed prescribe the consecration with five [mantras], beginning with the *akhaṇḍa*.
O Mistress of the Unmanifest (Akulanāyikā), place your free radiance here within the Supreme Nectar-Self, which bestows the bliss of undivided, singular flavor.
O Supreme One, who abides in the non-clan (akula), whose form is nectar, and who produces pure gnosis—
bestow the state of immortality upon this substance which has a moist form.
Having made that which possesses such form one with me, who possess this very nature, and having become the form of supreme nectar, cause the vibration of consciousness to manifest within me.
Thus, these three *anuṣṭubh* verses are the [three] knowledges (*vidyā*). Parks 3.28.
Then, having uttered "vācam blūṃ jhraum iti jūṃ saḥ," and [further] "amṛte amṛtodbhave amṛteśvari amṛtavarṣiṇi amṛtaṃ srāvaya srāvaya svāhā," this is the fourth mantra.

"Vāgbhava," "vada vada," then "vāgvādini," "vāṅmadanaklinne," "kledini," "kledaya," "mahākṣobhaṃ kuru," the pair "yugalaṃ mādanaṃ," "śaktiḥ," "mokṣaṃ kuru kuru"—this is the fifth *vidyā*, consisting of the fourteen-syllable and fifteen-syllable clusters along with the fourteen-syllable and sixteen-syllable clusters. Having consecrated [the water] with these, one should prepare that *arghya* as consisting of light. (Parks 3.30)

Having worshipped the sandals of the Guru on the head with those drops three times, one should offer that drop into the Kuṇḍalinī of oneself with the mantra: "I am the moist, blazing light; I am the light, I am Brahman; I who am, I am Brahman; I am, I am Brahman; I alone am I, I sacrifice myself, Svāhā! (Parks 3.31).
This is the purification of the *arghya* offering; may there be auspiciousness. (Parks 3.32)
4. Section:

The Lalitākrama Now, having caused the primordial consciousness—which resides in the heart-cakra, which is skilled at piercing the forest of lotuses within the suṣumnā, which has dispelled the darkness of delusion, and which is the radiance of the lamp of Śiva—to emerge through the right nostril, one should place that [consciousness], whose body is assumed through divine play, upon the crest of the *trikhaṇḍa* mudrā.
Having gathered a handful of flowers in his hand.

Having uttered "Māyā-lakṣmī Parā" and the name of the Goddess, one should perform the visualization with: "I visualize [her] as the embodiment of nectar and consciousness; obeisance. Thus having visualized. (Parks 4.2)
Having uttered the speech joined with *hasa* (the syllable *ha*), the sweet-toned *kalarī*, and also the fourteenth and sixteenth [vowels] joined with *hasa*, [one should say]:
"O Mother, O Supreme Goddess, who dwells within the Great Lotus Forest, whose form is the bliss of the Cause, and who is devoted to the welfare of all beings, come, come!"
Thus, having invoked the supreme consciousness (paraciti) into the Baindava-cakra.
One should perform the sixty-four types of offerings.
All offering mantras should be preceded by the Threefold Tārā and end with "kalpayāmi namaḥ. (Parks 4.4)
Having recited the *tritārī*, one should perform, in sequence: "I offer water for the feet; *namaḥ*"; the removal of ornaments; anointing with fragrant oil;
entry into the bathing hall; seating upon the jeweled throne in the bathing pavilion; divine bath-powders for rubbing; bathing with warm water;
the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) with all the holy waters poured from golden jars; wiping with a clean cloth; and dressing in a reddish silk garment (*aruṇadukūla*).

The donning of a saffron-colored upper garment; the entry into the pavilion for anointing; the sitting upon the jeweled throne in the pavilion for anointing; the smearing of all limbs with divine fragrances such as sandalwood, agallochum, saffron, musk, camphor, musk-pouch, and yellow orpiment;
the incense of black agallochum for the mass of hair; the garland of seasonal flowers—primarily jasmine, mālatī, jātī, campaka, aśoka, śatapatra, pūga buds, punnāga, and kalhāra;
the entry into the pavilion for ornaments; the sitting upon the jeweled throne in the pavilion for ornaments; and the new jewel-crown and crescent moon.
The vermilion for the parting of the hair, the jewel-tilaka, black collyrium, the pair of earlobes, the pair of jeweled earrings, the nose-ornament,
the lac-dye for the lips as the primary decoration, the golden cintāka, the padaka, the mahāpadaka, the pearl necklace, the single-string necklace,
the channavīra, the four pairs of armlets, the series of bracelets, the series of finger-rings, the girdle-belt, the waist-thread, and the auspicious ornament of marital bliss.

[She is adorned with] anklets, jeweled foot-ornaments, and toe-rings; in one hand a noose, in another an elephant-goad, in another a bow of sugarcane marked with the *puṇḍra*, and in another flower-arrows; [she wears] glorious ruby sandals; together with the attendant deities whose attire is identical to her own, she mounts the great discus and sits upon the couch on the lap of Kāmeśvara, [holding] a cup of nectar-wine and water for rinsing the mouth.

Having performed the sixty-four services with the words, "I offer camphor-rolls, joyful laughter of playful delight, the auspicious *ārārtika* lamp, the parasol, the pair of chowries, the mirror, the palm-leaf fan, perfume, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings; obeisance," [one should proceed]. (Parks 4.5)
And having displayed the nine mudrās.
Having satisfied [the deity] three times with the root mantra. // Parks_4.7 //
Having worshipped the six limbs of the Goddess in the directions of Agni, Īśa, Asura, and Vāyu, as well as in the center, and in the intermediate directions.
*vāksakalahrīṃ nityaklinne madadrave sauḥ*—this is Kāmeśvarī.
In all instances, the phrase *nityāśrīpādukā* should be appended.
*vāgbhagabhuge bhagini bhagodari bhagamāle bhagāvahe bhagaguhye bhagayoni bhaganipātini*.

O you who cause all to tremble with passion, O you whose form is the *bhaga*, O eternally moist one, O you whose very nature is the *bhaga*, bring to me all *bhagas*, O giver of boons! O you of excellent seed, O you of excellent seed, O you moistened by the *bhaga*, O you whose essence is moisture, make them wet, make them flow! O infallible one, O you who pierce the *bhaga*, agitate, cause agitation in all sentient beings! O Mistress of the *bhaga*! Aiṃ blūṃ jeṃ blūṃ bheṃ blūṃ moṃ blūṃ heṃ!
*Blūṃ heṃ klinne sarvāṇi bhagāni me vaśam ānaya strīṃ hara bleṃ hrīṃ bhagamālinī tāro māyā nityaklinne madadrave svāhā*— this is *Nityaklinnā*.
*Praṇavaḥ kroṃ bhroṃ krauṃ jhrauṃ chrauṃ jrauṃ svāhā*— this is *Bheruṇḍā*.
*Praṇava* (oṃ), *māyā* (hrīṃ), and "vahnivāsinyai namaḥ" constitute Vahnivāsinī. *Māyā* (hrīṃ), *klinne*, *vāk* (aiṃ), *kroṃ*, *nityamadadrave*, and *hrīṃ* constitute Mahāvajreśvarī.
*Māyā* (hrīṃ) and "śivadūtyai namaḥ" constitute Śivadūtī.
The Tvaritā [mantra] is: *praṇava* (oṃ), *māyā* (hrīṃ), *huṃ*, *khe*, *che*, *kṣaḥ*, *strīṃ*, *huṃ*, *kṣeṃ*, *hrīṃ*, *phaṭ*.
The Nityā [mantras] are: *Kumārī* and *Kulasundarī*; and *Vāgbhava* (*hasakalaraḍa*), *Bindumālinī* (*hasakalaraḍa*), and the fourteen and sixteen [syllables] (*hasakalaraḍa*).
*Māyā* (hrīḥ), *phreṃ*, *srūṃ*, *aṅkuśa-pāśa-smara-vāgbhava-blūṃ-pada-nitya-mada-drave*, *varma* (huṃ), *phreṃ*, and *māyā* (hrīḥ) constitute Nīlapatākā.
*Bha-ma-ra-ya-ūm* constitutes Vijayā. *Svaum* constitutes Sarvamaṅgalā.

*Tāro namo bhagavati jvālāmālini devadevi sarvabhūtasaṃhārakārike jātavedasi jvalanti jvala jvala prajvala prajvala trijātiyuktamāyārephasaptakajvālāmālini varmaphaḍagnijāyeti jvālāmālinī*. (Aṃ) *Ckaiṃ*— thus, in the *Citriṇī* [tradition], the fifteen Nityās are to be worshipped within the fifteen vowels situated upon the lines of the first triangle.
Having performed the dismissal, one should worship the Ṣoḍaśī with the root mantra.

In the center, having worshipped according to tradition the Pādukās—the Divine, Siddha, and Human Oghas—numbering thirty-four (34) within the previously mentioned triangle, one should thereafter worship the Lord upon one's own head;
this is the worship of the limbs of dissolution (*layāṅga-pūjana*). May there be auspiciousness! 4.10.
5. Section: Worship of the Ninefold Enclosure of Lalitā.
Now, in the first square [are worshipped] those ending with the attainment of all desires: *aṇimā*, *laghimā*, *mahimā*, *īśitva*, *vaśitva*, *prākāmya*, *bhukti*, *icchā*, and *prāpti*.

In the middle square [are worshipped] those beginning with Brāhmī and ending with Mahālakṣmī. In the third square [are worshipped] Saṃkṣobhaṇā, Drāvaṇā, Karṣaṇā, Vaśyā, Unmādanā, Mahāṅkuśā, Khecarī, Bījayoni, and Trikhaṇḍā.
All those former [images] are to be fully honored. // Parks_5.1 //

"May these manifest yoginīs in the Trailokyamohana-cakra—along with their mudrās, siddhis, weapons, śaktis, vehicles, and retinues—be well-honored with all ritual offerings. Having thus performed the collective worship of them, [one should proceed].
(Parks 5.2)
Having recited the Karaśuddhi mantra and touched the Mistress of the Tripura-cakra with the syllable *drām*, one should display the Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī mudrā.
The names of the Cakrayoginīs and the Mistress of the Cakra differ;
the rest is the same. (Parks 5.3)
On the sixteen-petaled [lotus] are Kāmākarṣiṇī, Nityākalā, and those ending with Nityākalā;

Buddhyākarṣiṇī, Ahaṅkārākarṣiṇī, Śabdākarṣiṇī, Sparśākarṣiṇī, Rūpākarṣiṇī, Rasākarṣiṇī, Gandhākarṣiṇī, Cittākarṣiṇī, Dhairyākarṣiṇī, Smṛtyākarṣiṇī, Nāmākarṣiṇī, Bījākarṣiṇī, Ātmākarṣiṇī, Amṛtākarṣiṇī, and Śarīrākarṣiṇī. These are the Guptayoginīs, together with their mudrās, in the Sarvāśāparipūraka-cakra, and so forth, as before, having recited the self-protection (*ātmarakṣā*).
Having worshipped Tripureśī, one should display the "drīṃ" [syllable], which causes all to be subdued.

Having contemplated these most secret Yoginīs— Kusumā, Mekhalā, Madanā, Madanāturā, Āveginī, Aṅkuśā, and Mālinī, preceded by Anaṅga— who are endowed with their respective *mudrās* in the *Sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇa-cakra*, and having recited the *ātma-āsana* as before,
one should worship Tripurasundarī and display the *Sarvākarṣiṇī-mudrā* while uttering "klīm. (Parks 5.5)

Having touched these [powers] beginning with Sarvā— Saṃkṣobhiṇī, Drāviṇī, Ākarṣiṇī, Āhlādinī, Saṃmohinī, Stambhinī, Jṛmbhiṇī, Vaśaṅkarī, Rañjanī, Unmādinī, Arthasādhinī, Sampattipūraṇī, Mantramayī, and Dvandvakṣayaṅkarī— the *sampradāya-yoginīs* together with their *mudrās* reside in the wheel that bestows all prosperity (*sarvasaubhāgyadāyakacakra*). Having recited the *cakrāsana* and worshipped Tripuravāsinī, the Mistress of the Wheel, [one should utter] "blūṃ."
One should display the mudrā that brings all under control. Parks_5.6 //

Having worshipped all those previously mentioned— Siddhipradā, Sampatpradā, Priyaṅkarī, Maṅgalakāriṇī, Kāmapradā, Duḥkhavimocinī, Mṛtyupraśamanī, Vighnanivāriṇī, Aṅgasundarī, and Saubhāgyadāyinī— in the outer ten-spoked wheel, these Kulottīrṇa Yoginīs, having spoken the remainder [of the mantra] in the Sarvārthasādhaka-cakra and having uttered the Mantra-āsanam while reflecting upon Tripurā Śrī Cakreśvarī, he should offer the Unmādinī-mudrā with the syllable *Saḥ*. (Parks 5.7)

In the inner ten-spoked wheel, those who bestow knowledge, power, and sovereignty; who consist of wisdom; who destroy disease; who are the nature of the support; who remove sins; who consist of bliss; who are the embodiment of protection; and who grant desired fruits—all these [deities] with their respective prefixes should be worshipped.

These are the *garbhayoginīs* in the wheel that effects all protection. Having likewise uttered the remaining [mantras], such as the seat of the *sādhya* and the *siddha*, one should honor Tripuramālinī and display the "KROM" of Sarvamahāṅkuśā. (Parks 5.8)

On the eight-spoked [wheel], the group of eight beginning with Vaśinī is worshipped; in the place of "namaḥ," the name of the worship mantra is inserted. These are the secret yoginīs in the wheel that removes all diseases.
Having recited the remaining portion clearly—the Mūrtividyā—and having propitiated Tripurāsiddhā, the Khecarī [mantra] "Śiva-bhṛgu-ṛddhi-yuk-phreṃ" should be given. 5.9.
Having uttered the seed-syllables of the arrows: "To all the expanding arrows, *namaḥ*! *Dhaṃ thaṃ*, to the bow that completely deludes all!

*Āṃ hrīṃ*, to the noose that brings all under control! *Kroṃ*, to the goad that paralyzes all! *Namaḥ*!"—thus is the worship of the weapons, beginning with the arrows, performed in the four directions outside the great triangle. (Parks 5.10)
In the triangle are the Great Goddesses Kāmeśvarī, Vajreśvarī, and Bhagamālinī, preceded by all [the letters] from *vāc*, *kāma*, and *śakti*; in the bindu is the fourth.
Immediately following these three, for the sake of non-differentiation, there is the worship of the Root Goddess (Mūladevī).

She is one and the same: she is the fourth among the Nityās beginning with Kāmeśvarī, the sixteenth among the goddesses of the wheels (*cakradevī*), and the ninth residing in the Bindu-wheel (*binducakra*).
One should not conceive of any distinction between the mantra and the deity therein.
That belongs specifically to the Great Goddess;
a special worship is performed at four locations. (Parks 5.12)
These are the most secret yoginīs in the wheel that bestows all accomplishments;
the remainder should be observed.
Having uttered the invocation and honored Tripurāmbā, the form of the seed-syllable and mudrā is *hsauṃ*. (Parks 5.13)

Having worshipped the Goddess with the root mantra in the *bindu-cakra*, [one should say]: "O you who are the Yoginī of the supreme and non-supreme secret, together with your mudrās, siddhis, weapons, powers (*śakti*), vehicles, and retinue—may you be fully worshipped with all ritual offerings (*upacāra*)! Then, having again uttered the root mantra and worshipped the Great Mistress of the Wheel (*mahācakreśvarī*), one should display the *yoni-mudrā* with the *vāgbhava* syllable.
As before, having offered incense, lamps, the mudrās, libations, food offerings, and so forth, // Parks_5.15 //
Having formed the face with one *bindu*, the breasts with two *bindus*, and the womb with the subsequent half [of the *bindu*], one should meditate upon her as the *kāmakalā*. // Parks_5.16 //
Having touched the Heart of Good Fortune. // Parks_5.17 //

On the left side, having prepared a triangle, a circle, and a square, and having honored them with perfumes and unbroken grains, one should utter the *vāgbhava* syllable and say, "Salutation to the pervasive maṇḍala," and then place there the first, intermediate, and final vessels filled with water mixed with half a portion of rice.
Having recited three times, "Oṃ hrīṃ, to all beings who create obstacles, huṃ svāhā," and having offered the bali-oblation... // Parks_5.19 //
Having gratified [him] with circumambulations, prostrations, recitations, and hymns of praise. // Parks_5.20 //

Having worshipped that single Śakti, who possesses that form, with the offerings appropriate for a young girl, and having gratified her with the fivefold offering (pañcaka), [one should proceed]. // Parks_5.21 //
Having offered the remainder of the oblation into the fire of consciousness together with the learned ones. // Parks_5.22 //
Having bound the khecarī-mudrā and saying "forgive me," one should release it and unite it within oneself; thus all is auspicious. (Parks 5.23)
6. Section: The Procedure of Śyāmā. This very [goddess] is the Great Vidyā, the Sovereign Empress, the Mistress of the Lion Throne; Śyāmā occupies the position of her chief minister.
One should always practice the contemplation of that sequence.
For it is indeed proper to seek the king's favor through the mediation of his chief ministers. // Parks_6.2 //

Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta* and remaining on his bed, he should bow to the venerable sandals (*śrīpādukā*), restrain his breath (*prāṇāyāma*), and contemplate the supreme consciousness (*parasaṃvid*) blazing from the *mūlādhāra* up to the *dvādaśānta*. Having mentally recited the root mantra three times and gone outside, having released his feces and urine, and having performed the cleansing of the teeth, the rubbing of the tongue, the spitting of phlegm, the purification of the nostrils, and twenty mouthfuls of water (*gaṇḍūṣa*), [he should proceed]. (Parks 6.3)
Having performed the desired ritual bathing with mantras, ashes, and water, and having put on a garment, [he should proceed].

Having performed the twilight worship, having visualized the Goddess with her retinue within the solar disc, and having offered three *arghya* oblations with the root mantra, he should satisfy them according to his capacity. (Parks 6.5)
Having entered the sacrificial hall and sat upon the seat with the mantra, "Obeisance to the lotus-seat of the foundational power (ādhāraśakti)," [he should remain seated]. Parks_6.6 //

Having placed his joined palms to his head with the words, "Obeisance to the Śrī-pādukās of the entire circle of manifest and secret Siddha-yoginīs," and having performed the worship of his own guru’s pādukās.

Having performed the placement [of the mantra] pervasively upon the palms, from the thumbs to the little fingers, on the two elbows, and on the body, using the weapon-mantra: *Aiṃ Hraḥ Astrāya Phaṭ*. (Parks 6.8)
Having drawn in the air with the syllable *yaṃ* through the *piṅgalā* and dried the body,
having drawn in the air with the syllable *raṃ* and burned the body, and having drawn in the air with the syllable *vaṃ* and sprinkled the ashes of the burnt body with nectar;
Having firmly drawn in the breath with "laṃ" and stabilized it, and having drawn in the breath with "haṃsa," one should generate the consciousness of Śiva. // Parks_6.9 //
Having uttered the root mantra once, one should draw in the breath; having uttered it three times, one should retain it (kumbhaka); and having uttered it once, one should exhale.
Having thus performed exhalation, inhalation, and retention three times, seven times, ten times, or sixteen times, one becomes a body composed of light.
Having performed the six-limbed ritual and having placed the Mātṛkā together with the Bāla-mantra upon the root, heart, and mouth, one should likewise place Rati, Prīti, and Manobhava.
Having divided the root [channel] into seventeen parts: six in the *brahmabila*, three in the forehead, four between the eyebrows, six in the right and left eyes,
eight and seven in the mouth, one each in the right and left ears and the throat, eight in the right and left shoulders,
ten in the heart, ten in the right and left breasts, eight and eight in the [sides of the] abdomen, nine at the navel, two in the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, and six in the *ādhāra*.
Having arranged [the deities] in this manner, // Parks_6.12 //
Furthermore, having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the seventeen sections, from the *ādhāra* up to the *brahmabila*, in the aforementioned locations. (Parks 6.13)

Having visualized a pavilion situated on a jewel-island in the midst of the ocean of nectar, adorned with strings of pearls and provided with four gates— at its four gates starting from the east— one should [place] *sāṃ* for Sarasvatī,
*lāṃ* for Lakṣmī,
and *śaṃ* for Śaṅkhanidhi.

Paṃ, obeisance to Padmanidhi; lāṃ, obeisance to Indra, who holds a thunderbolt in his hand, lord of the gods, whose vehicle is Airāvata, together with his retinue; rāṃ, obeisance to Agni, who holds a spear in his hand, lord of brilliance, whose vehicle is the goat, together with his retinue; ṭāṃ, obeisance to Yama, who holds a staff in his hand, lord of the departed spirits, whose vehicle is the buffalo, together with his retinue; kṣāṃ, obeisance to Nirṛti, who holds a sword in his hand...

Oṃ *vāṃ*, salutation to Varuṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas, who has a man as his vehicle, who holds a noose in his hand, the sovereign of the waters, accompanied by his retinue; *yāṃ*, salutation to Vāyu, who holds a banner in his hand, the lord of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), who has a ruru deer as his vehicle, accompanied by his retinue;
*sāṃ*, salutation to Soma, who holds a conch in his hand, the lord of the constellations, who has a horse as his vehicle, accompanied by his retinue.
Salutation to Hāṃ Īśāna, who holds a trident in his hand, the lord of knowledge, whose vehicle is the bull, together with his retinue;
salutation to Oṃ Brahmā, who holds a lotus in his hand, the lord of Satyaloka, whose vehicle is the swan, together with his retinue;
salutation to Śrīṃ Viṣṇu, who holds a discus in his hand, the lord of the serpents, whose vehicle is Garuḍa, together with his retinue; Oṃ, salutation to the Lord of the Site (Vāstupati).
With the words "Homage to Brahmā," one should worship the eleven deities in the eleven directions.
Regarding the mantras of the Śyāmā cycle, at the beginning there is the application of the Three Tārās with the Kumārī, or simply the Kumārī-yoga;
the "Three Tārās" are as previously stated, and "Kumārī" refers to Bālā; the remainder is self-evident.
With his limbs anointed with fragrant substances, his mouth perfumed with betel, and having become serene in mind, // Parks_6.16 //

Having drawn the king of wheels (*cakrarāja*)—consisting of a dot, a triangle, a pentagon, an eight-petaled lotus, a sixteen-petaled lotus, an eight-petaled lotus, a four-petaled lotus, and a square—upon mandalas of gold, silver, copper, sandalwood, or precious gems;
and having, with pure water consecrated by reciting the root mantra three times, formed a square, a circle, a hexagon, a triangle, and a dot using the entry-gesture (*praveśa-matsyamudrā*);
and having established the support (*ādhāra*) with the mantra: *aṃ ātmatattvāya ādhāraśaktaye vauṣaṭ*; [one should worship] Dhūmrārcis...

Having worshipped the fire-portions (agnikalā)— namely Ūṣmā, Jvalinī, Jvālinī, Visphuliṅginī, Suśrī, Surūpā, Kapilā, Havyavāhā, and Kavyavāhā— and having established the vessel with the mantra "Oṃ, to the Vidyātattva, to the lotus-faced one, vauṣaṭ," [one worships] within the vessel: Tapinī, Tāpinī,
Dhūmrā, Marīci, Jvālinī, Ruci, Suṣumnā, Bhogadā, Viśvā, Bodhinī, Dhāriṇī, and Kṣamā.

Having worshipped the digit of the Sun (sūryakalā) and filled [the vessel] with pure water while reciting "Oṃ, obeisance to the Śiva-principle, to the lunar orb," one should worship the lunar digits— Amṛtā,
Mānadā, Pūṣā, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Rati, Dhṛti, Śaśinī, Candrikā, Kānti, Jyotsnā, Śrī, Prīti,
Aṅgadā, Pūrṇā, and Pūrṇāmṛtā— in the southeast, northeast, southwest, northwest, in the center, and in the cardinal directions.

Having performed the placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), having protected [the site] with the weapon-mantra (*astra*), having enveloped it with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*), and having displayed the cow-seal (*dhenu-mudrā*) and the womb-seal (*yoni-mudrā*), one should consecrate it seven times with the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*). Then, having sprinkled the sacrificial hall and the articles of worship with droplets of that water— Parks_6.18 —

With those [mantras], having prepared a mandala consisting of a circle and a square marked with the letter *ī*, and having scattered flowers upon it, one should establish the support (*ādhāra*) as before, worship the digits of fire (*agnikalā*), and install the vessel (*pātra*). Within that vessel, [one recites]: *hrīṃ aiṃ mahālakṣmīśvari paramasvāmini ūrdhva-śūnyapravāhini somasūryāgnibhakṣiṇi paramākāśabhāsure*.

"Come, come! Enter, enter! Take, take the vessel! Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā! Having thus scattered a handful of flowers and worshipped the digits of the sun (sūryakalā), [one should offer the oblation] produced from the entire cosmic egg and filled with all essences.
Bring the nectar-essence that fills the great vessel.

Having thus filled the first [square] and placed the second, and having written the syllables *ha* and *la-kṣa* in the three corners marked by the three lines beginning with *a*, *ka*, and *tha*, and the syllable *haṃsa* in the center, one should consecrate it ten times with the root mantra, worship the digits of the moon (*candrakalāḥ*) in the southeast, northeast, southwest, northwest, and the center, as well as in the cardinal directions,
perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅgāni*), protect it with the weapon mantra (*astra*), and veil it with the armor mantra (*kavaca*).
One should display the source of the cow. // Parks_6.19 //

Having uttered "Śrīmātā" in the center of the *cakra* and fashioned the form with the mantra "Obeisance to the Form of Gīśvarī," and having again uttered "Śrīmātā" and invoked [her] with "I invoke the immortal consciousness of Gīśvarī," one should worship her with the sixteen offerings. Then, the limb-deities (aṅgadevīs) are to be worshipped in the directions of Fire, the Three-eyed One (Rudra), the Rakṣas, and the Wind, as well as around the head of the Goddess. Their mantras begin with "Sarvajana" and consist of eight, seven, eleven, ten, ten, and twenty-eight segments; they are accompanied by the *tritārī*, Kumārī, Vāk, and so forth, along with their respective classes and joined with the general *mudrās*.
Afterwards, one should perform the offering to the protective deities. // Parks_6.21 //

One should perform the worship of all the deities of the wheels by scattering unbroken grains and flowers from the right hand, accompanied by the first drop from the *śrīpātra* held between the thumb and ring finger of the left hand,
upon which Ratī, Prītī, and Manobhava are situated within the triangle.

At the base of the five spokes, in the sequence beginning from the front, [one should worship]: *drāṃ* to the Arrow of Melting, *drīṃ* to the Arrow of Drying, *klīṃ* to the Arrow of Binding, *blūṃ* to the Arrow of Deluding, and *saḥ* to the Arrow of Intoxication—*namaḥ*. In front of those, accompanied by *māyā*, *kāma*, *vāk*, *blūṃ*, and *strīm*, are Kāma, Manmatha, Kandarpa, Makaraketana, and Manobhava.

At the base of the eight petals, Brāhmī, Maheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Māhendrī, Cāmuṇḍā, and Caṇḍikā are to be worshipped, together with the vowels beginning with the final one (au) joined with the moon (bindu). In front of them are Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Rati, Prīti, Kīrti, Śānti, Puṣṭi, and Tuṣṭi. (Parks 6.25)

On the sixteen petals are Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Śānti, Śraddhā, Sarasvatī, Kriyāśakti, Lakṣmī, Sṛṣṭi, Mohinī, Pramathinī, Āśvāsinī, Vīcī, Vidyunmālinī, Surānandā, and Nāgabuddhikā. On the eight petals, one should meditate upon the Bhairavas—Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodhana, Unmatta, Kapāla, Bhīṣaṇa, and Saṃhāra—conjoined with Daṇḍin, Svara, and the pairs beginning with Ādi, ending with Bhairava.
On the four petals are Māyuktataṅgī and Siddhalakṣmī, as well as Mahāmāyuktataṅgī and Mahāsiddhalakṣmī.
Gaṃ Gaṇapati, Duṃ Durgā, Baṃ Baṭuka, Kṣaṃ Kṣetrapālas—these are to be worshipped in the square. (Parks 6.29)
Having worshipped there once again, beginning with "Salutation to Sarasvatī" and ending with "Salutation to Brahmā, the Lord of the Site" (vāstupati), [he should proceed]. (Parks 6.30)

Having worshipped the lineage gurus—who possess the form of the swan (*haṃsa*), who are filled with supreme light, and who are eternally compassionate—along the eastern line of the square [mandala]. (Parks 6.31)
One should worship the general and specific sandals upon one's own head.
Having again worshipped the Goddess and performed the sixteen services with the *bālā* mantra, // Parks_6.33 //

Having prepared a triangle, a circle, and a square with pure water, and having placed a vessel containing a base of half-cooked rice mixed with water, along with fragrant flowers, and its supporting stand—reciting "Śrīmātā," one says:

"Gīśvarī, take this offering, take it! Huṃ Phaṭ Svāhā! Having recited "Śrīmātā," one says: "Gīśvarī, protect me who has come for refuge! Protect me! Huṃ Phaṭ Svāhā! [And finally: "Kṣetrapālanātha, take this offering, take it! Phaṭ!"
Having offered the *bali* with the three mantras beginning with "Svāhā," while striking the left heel, clapping the hands, turning the face upward, and forming the *nārāca-mudrā*. (Parks 6.35)

Having summoned the dark-complexioned Śakti and worshipped her with the Bālā-mantra, having placed the beginning and end [of the mantra] upon her hand, having purified the reality (tattva), and having accepted the remainder of that, one should perform the daily worship together with worthy companions using the remnants of the oblation; and having performed one hundred thousand recitations (lakṣajapa), one should carry out the fire-offering (homa), the libation (tarpaṇa), and the feeding of Brahmins according to the sequence of one-tenth of that number. // Parks_6.37 //

A person should not cut down a *kadamba* tree, nor should they utter the word "Kālī. In assemblies involving lutes, flutes, dancing, singing, or recitation, one should not turn one's back, nor should one revile a singer. A lay follower of Lalita should not eat pieces of sugarcane, nor should he think of a female messenger by day; he should not loathe consecrated substances, nor should he treat women with harshness. He should not approach a hero’s wife, nor kill her, nor steal her property.
One should not voluntarily embrace the fivefold sensory world; one should not sit with those who have fallen from their lineage, nor engage in excessive chatter.

One should not walk along with a woman while she is conversing with another without joining the conversation oneself. One should protect the sacred books of the lineage. May there be auspiciousness! (Parks 6.39)
7. Section: The Vārāhīkrama.

Having thus worshipped the Mother of the Chants together with her limbs, one should worship Kola-mukhī, who stands as the commander-in-chief for the Great Queen Lalitā—who is seated upon the lion-throne of the empire of consciousness—and who possesses the wheel of unimpeded commands for the suppression of the wicked and the favoring of the virtuous, according to the conventions of the observance (samaya).
One should worship according to the prescribed rule. // Parks_7.1 //

In this regard, the sequence is as follows: having awakened during the great night, one should perceive the unstruck sound (*anāhata-dhvani*) resounding within the supreme space of one's own heart, which bestows intense bliss. (Parks 7.2)
"Salutation to Śiva and the other glorious gurus"—with these words, one should join the palms in reverence upon the head.
Having uttered the syllable "vācam" and "glauṃ," all the mantras in this manual are to be recited. (Parks 7.4)
One should purify the subtle body (liṅgadeha) with the six mantras beginning with the root mantra, according to the respective mantras. // Parks_7.5 //

From the root-triangle (*mūla-śṛṅgāṭaka*), through the path of Suṣumnā, I unite the individual Śiva (*jīva-śiva*) with the Supreme Śiva (*para-śiva*); *svāhā*. Yaṃ: dry up, dry up the contracted body; *svāhā*. Raṃ: burn, burn, cook, cook the contracted body; *svāhā*. Vaṃ: rain down, rain down the nectar of Supreme Śiva; *svāhā*. Laṃ: generate, generate the body of Śambhu; *svāhā*. Haṃsaḥ So ’ham: descend, descend!

"O soul, from the state of Śiva, enter the root-brain (mūla-śṛṅgāṭaka) by way of the suṣumnā path; shine forth, shine forth! blaze up, blaze up! burn brightly, burn brightly! Haṃsaḥ so 'haṃ svāhā!"—having thus performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the two *tārīs* encased by the *mātṛkās* upon the forehead, the two eyes, the two ears, the nose, the cheeks, the lips, the roots of the teeth, the head, the mouth, the two shoulders, the two feet, the joints, the tips, the two sides, the back, the navel, the abdomen, the heart, the base of the arms, the other [parts of the] throat, the armpits, the heart and so forth, the pair of hands and feet, the abdomen, and the face; // Parks_7.7 //
The five groups of seven syllables beginning with *andha* are assigned to the fingers from the thumb to the little finger.
Beginning with "vāṅ namo bhagavati," one worships the heart with thirteen [syllables],
the head with six,
and the crest-lock (śikhā) with ten.
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of armor, eyes, and weapons by means of seven [syllables] each, seven [each], and seven [each].
Having adorned it with perfumes and other offerings, one should purify the water for respectful reception (arghya).
Having smeared the front portion of the self with cow dung and drawn a square, a circle, a hexagon, and a triangle, one after another, with water mixed with the causal substances (*hetu*),
and having purified the supporting base and the offering vessel (*arghyapātra*) with the mantras for the purification of the *arghya* as taught in the Śyāmā-krama;
Having worshipped in general,
having extracted that *arghya* with the exclamation "vaṣaṭ," and having established it with "svāhā,"
Having enveloped [it] with "Hūṃ," having rendered it nectar with "Vauṣaṭ," and having protected it with "Phaṭ,"...
Having cast a flower with the word "namas," having gazed upon it with the root mantra, and having purified the articles of worship with its droplets; Parks 7.11.
(1) Having placed the previously mentioned groups of seven and five upon the head, face, heart, secret place, and feet,

(2) one should divide the Vidyā into eight parts and [place them] on the feet and so forth, the knees and so forth, the hips and so forth, the navel and so forth, the heart and so forth, the throat and so forth, the space between the eyebrows and so forth, and the forehead and so forth, up to the crown of the head.

Having placed the eleven syllabic segments—consisting of thirty-one, seven, seven, seven, seven, seven, and thirty-five—in the locations of the Mātṛkās, as well as the words of the root mantra; (3) Parks_7.12.
Having recited each of the eight previously mentioned segments individually, one should assign them to the aforementioned locations: *hlāṃ* to Śarva, the lord of the earth-element;
*hlīṃ* to Bhava, the lord of the water-element;
*hlūṃ* to Rudra, the lord of the fire-element.
Hlaiṃ to Ugra, lord of the wind element;
Hlauṃ to Īśāna, lord of the sun element; Soṃ to Mahādeva, lord of the moon element.

Haṃ to Mahādeva, the presiding lord of the principle of the sacrificer; Oṃ to Bhīma, the presiding lord of the principle of space; salutation—thus is the placement of the principles (tattvanyāsa). // Parks_7.13 //
Having performed the pervasive placement with the entire root mantra and having meditated upon the goddess, // Parks_7.14 //

In front [of him], having fashioned a boar-faced wheel (*kolamukhī-cakra*) made of cloth, silk, gold, silver, copper, sandalwood, or a pedestal, which is pleasing to the eye and characterized by three squares, a thousand petals, a hundred petals, eight petals, six spokes, five spokes, three spokes, and a central dot; // Parks_7.15 //
There, having scattered a handful of flowers, one should say: "Obeisance to the Golden Wall, to the Ocean of Nectar, to Varāhadvīpa, and to the Varāha-pīṭha.
Then: "Āṃ, obeisance to Ādhāraśakti; Kuṃ, obeisance to Kūrma."
Having worshipped on the pedestal with the sixteen mantras together with Dharma and the others, reciting: "Kaṃ to the bulb; Aṃ, obeisance to the infinite stalk. (Parks 7.16)
Having worshipped the wheel with the mantra of the wheel, saying: "Homage to the one seated upon the lotus-throne of three, five, six, eight, ten, and a hundred thousand petals. (Parks 7.17)

"Salutation to the fire-maṇḍala, salutation to the sun-maṇḍala, salutation to the moon-maṇḍala"—these are the three *guṇa-mantras*. Together with the four *ātma-mantras*, this twenty-sevenfold [set] is to be worshipped upon the seat (*pīṭha*).
"Hauṃ, obeisance to Sadāśiva, who is seated upon the corpse-lotus"—thus is the visualization of the Goddess's seat upon the wheel. (Parks 7.19)
"Ḷ Ṣā Ī Vārāhīmūrtaye Ṭhaḥ Ṭhaḥ Ṭhaḥ Ṭhaḥ Huṃ Phaṭ"— this is the Vidyā that effects the manifestation of the form, beginning with Vāgglauṃ and ending with Ādiglauṃ. (Parks 7.20)
Having performed the invocation, installation, bringing near, confinement, making face-to-face, veiling, salutation, the dhenu-mudrā, and the yoni-mudrā with the root-vidyā. (Parks 7.21)
He performed the six-limbed and five-limbed ritual placement upon the limbs of the Goddess.

At the conclusion of the arrangement of the sixteen services—namely, water for the feet (*pādya*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), bathing water, clothing, perfume, flowers, incense, lamps, the waving of lights (*nīrājana*), the parasol, the fly-whisk (*cāmara*), the mirror, the protective water for sipping (*rakṣācamanīya*), the food offering (*naivedya*), drinking water, and betel—[one should perform] meditation on the Goddess.

Vārtālī should be meditated upon as seated upon a lotus, dark as a rain-cloud, with curved fangs and tawny eyes, possessing full breasts, and holding in her hands a discus, sword, mace, the gesture of fearlessness, a conch, shield, plough, and the gesture of granting boons. Parks_7.23–24.
One should perform its satiation tenfold. (Parks 7.25)
In the triangle are Jambhinī, Mohinī, and Stambhinī. // Parks_7.26 //
And those [five] are Pañcārā, Andhinī, and Rundhinī. Parks_7.27.
In the hexagon: Ā KṢĀ Ī is Brahmāṇī;
Ī LĀ Ī is Māheśvarī; Ū HĀ Ī is Kaumārī.
Ṛ sā ī belongs to Viṣṇu; ai śā ī belongs to Indrāṇī;
au vā ī belongs to Cāmuṇḍā. At its front and in its center [are the syllables]: yamarayūṃ, yāṃ, yīṃ, yūṃ, yaiṃ, yauṃ, yaḥ. O Yākini, crush, crush! Seize, seize the skin-element of all my enemies!
"Bring [the powers of] *aṇimā* and so forth under control, bring them under control, svāhā!
For the other *dhātunāthās* as well, the mantra is formed in this way: by combining the seed-syllable, the name, and the element (*dhātu*) during the rite of propitiation.
"Ramarayūṃ! O Rākiṇī, drink, drink the blood-element! Lamarayūṃ! O Lākini, devour, devour the flesh-element!"

*Ḍamarayūṃ*, *Ḍākinī*, devour, devour the marrow element! *Kamarayūṃ*, *Kākinī*, crush, crush the bone element! *Samarayūṃ*, *Sākinī*, seize, seize the marrow element! *Hamarayūṃ*, *Hākinī*, drink, drink the semen element! Bring *aṇimā* and the other powers under control, *kuru kuru*, *svāhā*! Thus is the worship of the lords of the elements. (Parks 7.28)

Immediately thereafter, on both sides of the six spokes, are the two goddesses Krodhinī and Stambhinī, who hold chowries; there also are [the mantras]: "Homage to Stambhana-musala-āyudha" and "Homage to Ākarṣaṇa-hala-āyudha. Outside the six spokes, in front of the Goddess, is the worship of that [deity] with: "Kṣrauṃ Krauṃ, homage to Caṇḍoccaṇḍa. (Parks 7.29)
On the eight petals are Vārtālī, Vārāhī, Varāhamukhī, Andhinyā, and the others—these five. Outside of that: "Obeisance to the Great Buffalo, the vehicle of the Goddess. (Parks 7.30)
(1) On the hundred-spoked wheel, in front of the goddess, at the junction of the petals, [offerings] are made to Jambhinī, Indra, the Apsarases, the Siddhas, the twelve Ādityas,
Agni, the Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, Viśvakarman, Yama, the Mātṛs, the attendants of Rudra,
the Rudras, Mohinī, Nirṛti, the Rākṣasas, the Mitras, the Gandharvas, the hosts of Bhūtas, and Varuṇa.

Having worshipped the circle of deities with the mantra: "Homage to the Vasus, to the Vidyādharas, to the Kinnaras, to Vāyu, to Stambhinī, to Citraratha, to Tumburu, to Nārada, to the Yakṣas, to Soma, to Kubera, to the Devas, to Viṣṇu, to Īśāna, to Brahmā, to the Aśvins, to Dhanvantari, and to the Vināyakas. (2)

Outside of that, one should worship both with the mantra: "Oṃ Kṣauṃ, obeisance to the Guardian of the Field (Kṣetrapāla); obeisance to the Lion, the vehicle of the Goddess. Outside of that, the worship of that [next deity] is performed with: "Obeisance to the Great Black One, the King of Beasts, the vehicle of the Goddess. (Parks 7.31)

(1) On the thousand-spoked wheel divided eightfold, [one should perform] their external worship with the mantra: "Homage to Airāvata, Puṇḍarīka, Vāmana, Kumuda, Añjana, Puṣpadanta, Sārvabhauma, and Supratīka," or [the worship may be performed] from the ocean of nectar. (2) In the eight directions of the outer enclosure, as well as below and above, are Hetuka and the others.
Each of the [deities] beginning with Kṣauma should be worshipped accompanied by the names Bhairava and Kṣetrapāla.
The ten Bhairavas are Hetuka, Tripurāntaka, Agni, Yamajihva, Ekapāda, Kālakarāla, Bhīmarūpa, Hāṭakeśa, Acala, and [the tenth]. (Parks 7.32)
Having thus worshipped the six enclosures, and having again gratified the Goddess in three ways, he should serve her with all the ritual offerings.

In front, on the left side, having smeared an area of one cubit with water, one should prepare ten balls the size of a cock's egg by mixing blood-rice, turmeric-rice, buffalo meat, parched grain flour, sugar, the three causal fruits, honey, the three types of *mudga* beans, black gram flour, curd, milk, and ghee, along with boiled rice; having placed these there, one should deposit near them a single ball the size of a wood-apple (*kapittha*),
as well as a cup containing the *sādi*, *upādi*, and *madhyama* [substances], and offer the ten balls to Hetuka and the others.
Having offered the middle portion of the sacrificial cake and the cup to Caṇḍoccaṇḍa with their respective mantras, one should worship the Vṛnda.
Having satisfied the glorious guru according to one's means. // Parks_7.35 //

Having summoned three Śaktis who were in the full bloom of youth, endowed with auspicious marks, and intoxicating with passion, and having likewise honored and bathed a single Baṭuka, he adorned them all with perfumes and other offerings. Then, regarding one Śakti as Vārtālī and the other two as Krodhinī and Stambhinī, he placed the one in the center and the other two on either side; and regarding the Baṭuka as Caṇḍoccaṇḍa, he stationed him in front. Having satisfied them all with every kind of substance, he proceeded.
He should reply to them, "May I attain the accomplishment of the mantra of Śrīvārtālī," and they should say, "May the presiding deities be gracious."

Thus, having propitiated the noble goddess Bhūdāravadanā together with her retinue, and having performed one hundred thousand recitations as the preliminary service (*puraścaraṇa*), one should accomplish the mantra by offering oblations of *tāpiccha* flowers amounting to a tenth part of that number.
Then, having united the worshipped goddess with oneself, one may dwell at will; having attained mastery over commands, one shall live happily. May there be auspiciousness!

8. Khaṇḍa: Having performed the ritual service (*varivasyā*) to Vārtālī according to the rules, one should contemplate the unsurpassed heart-essence of the *siṃhāsana* vidyā—the abode in the form of the supreme seed-syllable (*parābīja*), preceded by its sequential order. (Parks 8.1)
For one who knows the heart of the Lord, there are joys at every step. // Parks_8.2 //
Now, we shall explain the method for the unsurpassed [attainment]. // Parks_8.3 //

Having arisen at dawn and meditated upon her body—overflowing with the spreading streams of nectar dripping from the pair of feet of the Supreme Goddess (Parā), who is golden-hued and seated within the thousand-petaled lotus in the hollow of the Brahma-ādhāra—[he should perform his rites]. (Parks 8.4)
Having bathed and put on clean garments, having sipped water three times with a golden vessel and wiped his mouth twice.
Having touched [the organs] once—
the eyes and the nostrils—
In the ear, the shoulder, and the navel.
Having touched his heart and his head,
and having thus sipped water three times. // Parks_8.5 //
Having occupied a seat made of the softest and purest wool, consecrated with golden, solar, and japā-mantras, and sprinkled with the root mantra. // Parks_8.6 //
With a joyful countenance, silent, and his body adorned, he worshipped the Teacher at the head with the mantra *mūlapūrveṇa*. // Parks_8.7 //
Having dispelled the obstructors residing in the netherworlds and other realms—who appear as manifestations of duality—by striking the left heel and snapping the fingers three times. (Parks 8.8)
Having performed the placement of the root mantra upon the head, face, heart, base, and all the limbs.
Having drawn in the breath through the mouth shaped like the beak of a crow and recited the root mantra twenty-seven times, one should seal the object of knowledge at the navel;

then, having recited it another twenty-seven times and tied the topknot with the thumb, one should again fill the breath, thereby ignite the fire of consciousness (cidagni) at the root, and contemplate the dissolution of the object of knowledge therein. // Parks_8.10 //

On a square ground surface smeared with cow dung, having formed the circles of earth, space, air, and fire using the "fish-seal" (*matsyamudrā*) gesture made with the hands moving along the sides and joined with water scented with divine fragrance,
one should place the general and specific *arghya* offerings as in the case of Śyāmā.
All [the names] should also be made with the syllable *sauḥ* preceding them, followed by the names of the heroic ones (*parākramamanu*). Parks_8.13 //
Having performed the six-limbed ritual for the *bhṛgu* syllables by repeating them fourteen, sixteen, and twice;
the six-limbed ritual for the phonemes by repeating the entire root mantra six times;
and likewise the six-limbed ritual for the mantra. // Parks_8.14 //
Having honored both [of them]. // Parks_8.15 //
Having recited the root mantra,
[one should meditate on] her who consists of consciousness, whose characteristic is bliss, who holds a jar of nectar and a piece of meat in her two hands,
and who is serene.
Having worshipped the Goddess Sudhā with the mantra "I worship the Goddess; obeisance, svāhā," he sprinkles the articles for the ritual service with that [water]. 8.16.

Having brought the aggregate of the thirty-six principles—which was previously sealed at the navel and dissolved into the fire of consciousness like molten iron—into the lotus of the heart; Parks_8.17 //

One should perform the arrangement of the seat by casting flowers consecrated with the root-mantra and the mantras to be mentioned hereafter, beginning with "Oṃ, obeisance to the Yoga-pīṭha starting with the Root" (mūlādiyogapīṭhāya namaḥ) and ending with the following: Earth, Water, Fire, Air, Space; Smell, Taste, Form, Touch, Sound; the Organs of Generation, Excretion, Feet, Hands, Speech; the Nose, Tongue, Eyes, Skin, Ears;
Ahaṃkāra, Intellect, Mind; Prakṛti, Puruṣa, Niyati, Kāla, Rāga, Kalā, Vidyā, Māyā, Śuddhavidyā, Īśvara, Sadāśiva, Śakti, and Śiva.
Having thus formed the *parācakra* [mudrā], // Parks_8.18 //
There, having invoked the supreme Goddess, who consists of sixteen digits and whose nature is the reflective awareness of that unity.
May the Supreme Art (Paramā Kalā) protect me— she who possesses the luster of the stainless moon, who has three eyes, who holds the crescent moon, and whose beautiful arms bear the seal and the book.
Having meditated thus. // Parks_8.20 //

Having recited the root [mantra], one should worship the Supreme Goddess (Parābhaṭṭārikā) in the form of Light at the root; having recited the middle of the root, the Supreme Goddess in the form of Reflection (vimarśa); and having recited the end of the root, the Supreme Goddess in the form of both Light and Reflection—at these three locations, the root, the heart, and the mouth of the Goddess, one should worship her and then recite the entire [mantra].

Having contemplated that very Goddess— who is the Supreme Sovereign (Parābhaṭṭārikā) consisting of great light and self-reflexive awareness— ten times, one should meditate upon her as blazing like ten million fires of cosmic destruction. // Parks_8.21 //
In that [state], having offered all that is to be known by means of the utterance of ritual action, // Parks_8.22 //
Having recited the root mantra, one should offer the *arghya* to the Guru situated upon one's own head by means of the general *pāduka*. // Parks_8.23 //
Again, having visualized the fire of consciousness as blazing, // Parks_8.24 //
Having worshipped the three sandals of the Divine Current (divyaugha), the three of the Siddha Current (siddhaugha), and the eight of the Human Current (mānavaugha).
The venerable Mother Parābhaṭṭārikā, along with Ghorā, Śrīkaṇṭha, Śaktidhara, Krodha, Tryambaka, Ānanda, Pratibhādevī, and Ambā;
the venerable Mother Madhurādevī, who is the sweet nectar of the consciousness of heroes (vīrasaṃvidānanda); and Jñānaśrī, Rāma, and Yoga.
They were sandals of valor. // Parks_8.26 //
Then, having offered the oblation with the *kalā* mantra, // Parks_8.27 //
One should appropriate for oneself the remainder of the oblation.
Thus may there be auspiciousness. (Parks 8.28)
9. Section: The Ritual for Homa. Now we shall explain the ritual procedure for the homa of one’s own chosen mantra. Parks_9.1 //
Having prepared either a square sacrificial pit or a leveled altar (sthaṇḍila) one cubit in length and raised by a thumb's breadth. // Parks_9.2 //
Having purified the general offering water (arghya) and having sprinkled [the area] with it.
Having drawn three lines facing east and three facing north. // Parks_9.4 //
Having worshipped Brahmā, Yama, Soma, the Maruts, Viṣṇu, and Indra within those lines, enshrined within the "namaḥ" mantra of the six Tārās; // Parks_9.5 //
Sahasrārciṣe hṛdayāya namaḥ; Svastipūrṇāya śirase svāhā;
Utiṣṭha puruṣāya śikhāyai vaṣaṭ.

Having performed the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with the mantras: *dhūmavyāpine kavacāya hūṃ*, *saptajihvāya netratrayāya vauṣaṭ*, and *dhanurdharāya astrāya phaṭ*, one should worship the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with those six limbs.

There, having drawn the fire-wheel (*agnicakra*) consisting of an eight-cornered, six-cornered, and three-cornered [figure], one should worship the pedestal-energies (*pīṭhaśakti*) of the fire in the center of the triangle with the mantra: "Obeisance to Pītā, Śvetā, Aruṇā, Kṛṣṇā, Dhūmrā, Tīvrā, Sphuliṅginī, Rucirā, and Jvālinī. Then, [one worships] that [fire] with the mantra *tamas*.
Raṃ to Rajas;
Saṃ to Sattva;
Ām to the Self (Ātman).
One should worship right there with the mantra: "Am, salutation to the inner self; Paṃ, salutation to the supreme self; Hrīṃ, salutation to the self of knowledge. (Parks 9.7)

Then, having worshipped Vāgīśvarī and Vāgīśvara—the parents of the fire about to be born—upon the pedestal, and having meditated upon their union, one should contemplate with the mantra: *hrīṃ namaḥ vāgīśvarīvāgīśvarābhyām*.

Having produced the fire from a fire-drill (*araṇi*), a sun-crystal (*sūryakānta*), or the house of a twice-born, and having placed it in an earthen or copper vessel in the southeast, northeast, or southwest, one should cast away the portion of the fire that is the "flesh-eater" (*krāvyādāṃśa*) toward the southwest, and then [purify the fire] by means of inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*), sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), striking (*tāḍana*), veiling (*avakuṇṭhana*), and so forth.
Having purified [it], one should utter: "Oṃ vaiśvānara jātaveda ihāvaha lohitākṣa sarvakarmāṇi sādhaya svāhā.

Then, having caused the consciousness that has risen from the *mūlādhāra* to emerge through the gateway of the eye in the forehead, one should cause it to fall into union with the external fire. (Parks 9.9)
Having covered it with fuel using the armor mantra (kavaca-mantra).
I pay homage to Agni, the blazing one, the knower of all beings, the consumer of oblations;
to the golden-hued Anala, the kindled fire whose faces are turned in every direction.
Having thus paid homage, [he said]. Parks 9.11.
"Arise, O greenish-brown one with red eyes! Accomplish all my rites! Grant [the goal] and cause it to be granted! Svāhā!"—having thus raised the fire. (Parks 9.12)
"Citpiṅgala, slay, slay! Burn, burn! Cook, cook! By the command of the Omniscient One, svāhā! Having thus kindled [the fire], // Parks_9.13 //

Having performed the rites of *puṃsavana*, *sīmanta*, *jātakarman*, *nāmakaraṇa*, *annaprāśana*, *caula*, *upanayana*, *godāna*, and *vivāha* with the six-syllable mantra accompanied by the word "namas," [reciting]: "By means of the fire named so-and-so, I perform such-and-such a rite; namas!"—thus he should proceed. (Parks 9.14)
Having sprinkled [water] around, having strewn [grass] around, and having laid the enclosing sticks around.
Three-eyed, with a reddish glow, his crown bound, possessing a very white parrot and a red one, adorned with many ornaments, seated upon a lotus,
and holding in his hands the desired boons, power, the svastika, and the gesture of fearlessness.
Bow down to Kṛśānu, whose shoulders are adorned with a golden garland.
Having meditated thus. // Parks_9.16 //

(1) In the eight corners: "Obeisance to Jātavedas, to Saptajihva, to Havyavāha, to Aśvodara, to Vaiśvānara, to Kaumāratejas, to Viśvamukha, and to Devamukha. (2) In the six corners: the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*).
(3) In the triangle: having worshipped Agni with the fire-mantra. // Parks_9.17 //

One should offer seven oblations into the seven tongues of Agni with clarified butter purified by the root-mantra, using the formula: "Homage to Hiraṇyā, Kanakā, Raktā, Kṛṣṇā, Suprabhā, Atiraktā, and Bahurūpā.
