Then, having performed three oblations for Agni with the verses beginning "O Vaiśvānara, arise" and "O tawny one," one should proceed. (Parks 9.19)
Having invoked the chosen deity upon the tongue of Bahurūpa and having honored it with the five types of offerings, // Parks_9.20 //

Having offered one oblation for all the goddesses of the wheels, one should perform the remaining mantras—ending with "namas" and "pādukā"—by adding "svāhā" at the end and then offer them as oblations. // Parks_9.21 //
Then one should offer ten oblations to the principal deity.

If he should desire something desired, having made a declaration to his chosen deity and formed a formal resolve (saṅkalpa), he should think: "For the sake of accomplishing this much of the rite, I shall perform this many oblations. Parks_9.23.
With sesame and clarified butter for peace; with cooked rice for the attainment of food; with *samidh* wood and mango sprouts for the pacification of fever; with *dūrvā* grass for longevity;
with *kṛtamāla* flowers for wealth; with blue lotuses for fortune; with *bilva* leaves for sovereignty; with lotuses for kingship; with pure parched grains for imperial rule;
with *nandyāvarta* flowers for a daughter; with *vañjula* flowers for poetic talent; with jasmine, *jātī*, and *puṇnāga* flowers for nourishment; and with [other offerings] for good luck.

For sovereignty, one should use bandhūka, japā, kiṃśuka, bakula, and madhuka flowers; for attraction, salt; for total subjugation, kadamba flowers; for grain, rice grains; for good fortune, fragrant substances such as saffron and gorocana; for splendor, palāśa flowers or tawny butter;
for madness, dhattūra flowers; and for [destruction], poisonous trees or fuel-sticks of nimba, śleṣmātaka, and vibhītaka.

One should offer oblations with salt smeared with neem oil for the destruction of enemies; with the feathers of a crow and an owl for killing; with black pepper smeared with sesame oil for causing enmity; and for the destruction of cough and asthma, one should offer oblations [with the same materials]. (Parks 9.24)
Having offered the bali-oblation. // Parks_9.25 //
Oṃ bhūr! To Agni and to the Earth and to the Great One, svāhā!
Oṃ bhuvaḥ! To Vāyu and to the Intermediate Space and to the Great One, svāhā!
Oṃ suvaḥ! To Āditya and to Heaven and to the Great One, svāhā!
Having performed the Mahāvyāhṛti-homa with these four mantras: "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, svāhā to the Moon, to the constellations, to the quarters, and to the Great One," [Parks 9.26].

Whatever has been thought, spoken, or done by me through mind, speech, or action— with the hands, feet, belly, or genitals— due to the influence of vital breath, intellect, body, or duty, in the states of waking, dreaming, or deep sleep; may all that be an offering to Brahman, Svāhā!
Thus, having performed the oblation of the offering to Brahman. // Parks_9.27 //
"Having dismissed the deity, the fire of consciousness, within myself with the words 'Obeisance,' I perform the ritual dismissal. Thus [it is said]. Parks 9.28.
Wearing that ash-mark as a tilaka, he who causes the delusion of the world may wander happily. May there be auspiciousness! (Parks 9.29)
10. Section: The Common Procedure for All.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the general method for all mantras. Parks_10.1 //
As in the case of Śyāmā, [the procedure] from the twilight offerings up to the purification of the arghya water is performed, excluding the ritual placement (nyāsa). // Parks_10.2 //
For one who has not been taught the six limbs, the six-limbed [mantra] is formed through the illusion of being endowed with the six classes.
The wheel consists of a dot, three spokes, six spokes, eight petals, four petals, and a square.
In the *bindu* are the primary deity’s powers of will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and action (*kriyā*);

in the triangle are the respective six limbs; in the six-spoked wheel are Brāhmī and the others; and in the eight-petaled lotus are Gaṇapati, Durgā, Baṭuka, and Kṣetrapāla; in the four-petaled lotus are Gaṇapati, Durgā, Baṭuka, and Kṣetrapāla.
In the square [are] the guardians of the directions. Parks_10.5 //
All the mantras of the Krama should be employed with the two syllables *tritārī* and *kumārī*. // Parks_10.6 //
Invocation is performed with the root mantra of each respective deity; the bali offering is made with the kalā-mantra, and the oblation is offered according to this sequence.
Now follows the Raśmimālā. Parks_10.8 //
This should be recited once with the mind by one who has arisen from sleep. (Parks 10.9)
(1) The Praṇava: Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ.
We meditate upon that most excellent splendor of the divine Savitṛ;
may he impel our intellects.
Thus, the Gāyatrī consists of thirty syllables.
(2) O Indra, from whatever we fear, grant us freedom from that fear. O Maghavan, be able to help us for our protection; slay our enemies and those who oppose us.
Bestower of well-being, lord of the people, slayer of Vṛtra, dispeller of foes, the self-controlled one—
may Indra, the bull, go before us, the giver of well-being and the creator of fearlessness.
Thus ends the Aindrī [mantra], consisting of sixty-seven syllables, which destroys fear in times of distress.
(3) "Praṇava," "ghṛṇi," "sūrya," and "āditya"—this eight-syllable mantra dedicated to the Sun bestows splendor.
The *praṇava* alone is the knowledge of Brahman that bestows liberation.
(5) Tāraḥ, parorajase, 'sāv ad, oṃ— this nine-syllabled Turyagāyatrī reflects upon its own identity with the Fourth State.
This pentad of rays should be contemplated as the seed-syllables located at the root, the heart, the forehead, the aperture of Brahmā, and the twelve-finger space above the head.
(1) Homage to the one whose splendor is like the eye of the sun.
(2) Homage to the sky-walker.
(3) Lead me from non-existence to existence.
(4) Lead me from darkness to light; (5) lead me from death to immortality;
(6) the Blessed One is warm and pure in form.
(7) The Blessed One is a swan, pure and peerless.
The one of universal form, the compassionate, the knower of all beings, the golden, the sole light, burning intensely;
he who possesses a thousand rays, existing in a hundred ways.
This sun rises as the vital breath of all creatures.
[259] (9) Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, the Sun! O carrier, O carrier! O carrier, O carrier! Svāhā!
(10) Birds with beautiful wings, the Priyamedha seers, have approached Indra with a longing for help:
"Dispel the darkness; fill our vision!"
Deliver us, who are bound like those caught in a snare.
(11) Homage to the lotus-eyed one. (12) Homage to the one with eyes like a lotus. (13) Homage to the one with stainless eyes.
(14) Salutation to the lotus-eyed one.
(15) Salutation to the one of universal form. (16) Salutation to the illustrious Mahāviṣṇu.
Thus is the Cākṣuṣmatī Vidyā, which bestows far-reaching vision and consists of the collective essence of sixteen mantras. // Parks_10.11 //
"O Viśvāvasu, king of the Gandharvas, grant me the maiden who is my heart's desire; then [the word] 'Agnivallabhā' is the vidyā that bestows the marriage of an excellent maiden. (Parks 10.12)
"Tāro namo rudrāya pathiṣade svasti mā sampāraya" is the mantra that removes dangers on the road. // Parks_10.13 //
Having uttered the words *tāre tāre pada*, followed by the sounds *tuttāre ture* and *dahanadayite*, this is the vidyā that extinguishes water.
"Obeisance to Acyuta, obeisance to Ananta, obeisance to Govinda"— this is the threefold knowledge of names that destroys great diseases. (Parks 10.15)
These five rays are to be elaborated as the retinue beginning with the root.

The Praṇava, Kamalā, Bhuvanā, Madana, Glā, the fourteenth and fifteenth [vowels], Gaṃ, "to Gaṇapati," the pair of Varas, Da, "may all people," the word Me, Vaśam Ānaya, Agni, and Vāmalocanā—this is the Mahāgaṇapati-vidyā, which pacifies all obstacles. (Parks 10.17)
The syllable *praṇava* [followed by] "namas śivāyai," and again "praṇava namas śivāyai"— this twelve-syllabled mantra is the Vidyā that reflects upon the Śiva-tattva. (Parks 10.18)
The ten-syllable mantra—*praṇava*, *kāṣṭha*, *madakṣa*, *śruti*, *bindu*, *piṇḍa*, *bhṛgu*, *ṣoḍaśa*, *mām*, and *pālayadvandvam*—is this knowledge that is death even unto death. (Parks 10.19)

*Tāraḥ* (Oṃ), *namo brahmaṇe*, "May there be retention for me; may there be no forgetting; may I be a retainer. What has been heard by my ears, let that not depart from me, [the hearing] of such-and-such a person, Oṃ. This is the *vidyā* known as the Retainer of What is Heard (*śrutadhāriṇī*). All the phonemes beginning with *śrīkaṇṭha* (Ś) and ending with *kṣa*, accompanied by the *bindu*, constitute the *mātṛkā*; this is the *vidyā* that brings about omniscience.
The five rays, consisting of the protection beginning with the root [mantra], are to be worshipped. // Parks_10.22 //

Śiva, Śakti, Kāma, Kṣiti, Māyā, Ravi, Indu, Smara, Haṃsa, Purandara, Bhuvana, Aparā, Manmatha, Vāsava, and Bhauvana—this is the Vidyā beginning with Śiva, which reflects upon its own essential nature. (Parks 10.23)

From the syllable *kla*, there is one *bindu* of the left eye; another consists of the *bindus* of the infinite source (*anantayoni*); and yet another is the emission from the trident of Śaṅkara’s supreme power (*parātriśūla*). These very same [syllables] in reverse order form the six-peaked (*ṣaṭkūṭā*) *sampatkarī* mantra. Having uttered this, one says "svāhā" for the eternal creation (*sṛṣṭinitye*), and "ham" for the full maintenance (*sthitipūrṇe*), followed by "namaḥ. Then, for the great destroyer of fire-bindus (*analabindumahāsaṃhāriṇī*), one says "kāli phaṭ" at the foot of the syllable *kṛśe*. This is the seed-syllable of the seventh seal (*mudrā*) of the fire-bindu, known as the Great Name (*mahānākhye*), belonging to Ananta-Bhāskari.

From the word *mahācaṇḍapad*, [the mantra] *kāli phaṭ* is formed; this is the seed-syllable of the Khecarī, which represents the reverse order of creation, maintenance, and withdrawal, as well as the Great Caṇḍa Speech and Yogīśvarī.
Thus, she who embodies the fivefold Vidyā is Kālasaṅkarṣiṇī, the bestower of supreme longevity. (Parks 10.25)
The three *tārīs*, the seventh mudrā, Śiva conjoined with Śakti, and the pair *ahaṃ*—these five constitute the *lomya*; this is the *śāmbhavī* vidyā, consisting of pure knowledge. 10.26.
The discharges of Bhṛgu’s trident constitute supreme knowledge. Parks_10.27 //
These five rays are to be conceived as being based upon the root and the other [stations]. // Parks_10.28 //
The powers of speech and desire, proceeding both in direct and reverse order, then proceed again in direct order; such is the power of the limbs of Śrī. (Parks 10.29)
"Bhuvana, Kamalā, Subhagā, Tārā, Obeisance to the Blessed One, O Pūrṇā, O Crest-Jewel! Having spoken thus, 'Grant me my desired food, O Daughter of Fire!'—this is the *Śri-upāṅga*, Annapūrṇā.

The *Praṇava* (Oṃ), the three syllables beginning with *Pāśa* (Hrīṃ), having spoken 'Come, O Supreme Goddess,' followed by the expression 'O Goddess with the Left Eye of Fire'—this is the *Śri-pratyaṅga*, Aśvārūḍhā."
The seventh mudrā is the *tāritrika*: *śiva-śakti-saṃvarta-puñca-ma-purandara-vara-yūṃ*, followed by *śakti-śiva-kṣamā* at the end, then *vādi-vara-yīṃ*;

then *śiva-bhṛgu-triśūla-bindu-bhṛgu-śiva-triśūla-visṛṣṭayaḥ*, preceded by *śrī* and the name of one's own guru, and finally the eight-syllabled mantra (*aṣṭākṣarī*) and the *śrīpādukā*. (Parks 10.32)
Endowed with these four, that sovereign Root-Vidyā is to be beheld in the Mūlādhāra. (Parks 10.33)
"To Mādana, Śakti, Bindu, Mālinī, Vāsava, Māyā, Ghoṣa, Doṣākara, Kandarpa, Gaganamaghavat, Bhuvana, Bhṛgu, Puṣpabāṇa, and Bhūmā—this is her Great Knowledge (mahāvidyā). (Parks 10.34)
The goddess Laghuśyāmā has a dark body and beautiful eyes like fire; she is the subduer of all through her speech, and she utters "O Mother, O Cāṇḍālī of the remnants. Parks_10.35 //
Having uttered "Kumārī," one should recite the pair "vada vada" and the word "vāk" for the disputant; then "vahnipriyā" is the subsidiary part (upāṅga) of Śyāmā, [forming] Vāgvādinī. 10.36.
The syllable Om, the bow, the arrow, the bull, the sacrificial grass, and the words "svāhā" and "vaṣaṭ"—these are the ornaments upon his head, fashioned from the essence of the fire-altar;
Nakuli and Śyāmā adorn every limb. (Parks 10.37)
In the place of the triad beginning with Lalitāpādukā, Kumārī should be joined; the rest is as before—this is Śyāmāpādukā. (Parks 10.38)
In the heart-cakra, Śyāmā, joined with four [mudrās], is to be worshipped.

The knowledge of that [mantra] is the *Tritārī-Kumārī*, consisting of ninety-eight syllables, beginning with the six seed-syllables (*bīja*) of the mantra in reverse order: *tadvidyā* (the knowledge of that), *tritārī* (the three *Tārās*), *kumārī* (the Virgin), *nabhavaśrītaṃśvasajamahāsamuraṃnimāyāsarāvakasastrīruvakasadumṛvakasasavakasalovakaakaṃvamāyahāvarṇāḥ*, *oṃmogatimāgīrirvananorirvakhajimadanaśrīṃrvajaśaṃrirvapuṣaśaṃrirvaṣṭagaśaṃrirvatvaśaṃrirvakaśaṃrimumeśanasvānta*. Thus ends the section on the sixty seed-syllables in reverse order. (Parks 10.40)

Hara with the bindu, Vā (the letter Va) preceded by Ā, Sthāṇu with the bindu, the word for "madman" (unmatta), the word "Bhai," and "Obeisance to the sandals of the Sun"—this is the Laghu-Vārtālī, the limb of the Vārtālī [mantra]. (Parks 10.41)

"Vedādibhuvanam," "namo vārāhi ghore," "svapnaṃ ṭha dvitayam," and "agnidārā"—this is the *upāṅga* of Vārtālī; Svapnavārtālī is she who speaks of the fruits of good and evil in dreams. (Parks 10.42) "Vāg hṛdayaṃ bhagavati tiraskariṇi mahāmāye," "paśupadāt janamanaścakṣustiraskaraṇaṃ kuru dvitayam," "varma phaṭ," and "pāvakaparigraha"—this is the *pratyaṅga* of Vārtālī;
[she is] Tiraskariṇī. (Parks 10.43)
Having omitted the three seed-syllables beginning with the mantra of Śyāmāpādukā, one should employ "vāg glaum";
this is Vārtālīpādukā. (Parks 10.44)
Endowed with these sciences, this Blessed Lady, whose face is like the opening of the earth, is to be worshipped in the wheel of time.

Manu said this: "Iyaḥ, ayaṃ, vākpuṭitaṃ, glauṃ, nabha, vavāli, rtāvā, hirā, vahakhi, rāmuaṃaṃnimaḥ, dhedhinajaṃjaṃnimaḥ, hehinastaṃstaṃnimaḥ, rvaṣṭadunāṃ, rvesavākttakṣukhati, hvābhakukuśī—these words are endowed with the sounds *va*, *ti*, *rtā*, *vā*, *li*, *rā*, *vā*, *hi*, *rā*, *mu*, *va*, *khi*, *dhe*, *dhi*, *na*, *ruṃ*, *ruṃ*, *nimaḥ*, *bhe*, *bhi*, *namaḥ*, *mo*, *nimaḥ*, *bhe*, *bhi*, *nasadu*, *praṣṭā*, *saṣāṃ*, *rvaci*, *rmuga*, *jistaṃnaṃ*, *ru*, *ghraṃ*, *śyaṃ*. Thus it is accompanied by these sounds.
"Vāk glauṃ," followed by the seven ending with "visṛṣṭi," then four times "varmāstrāya phaṭ"—this [mantra] consists of one hundred and twelve syllables. (Parks 10.46)
The Śrīpūrti-vidyā, which is indeed Śrī herself with the fifth and eleventh seed-syllables removed, is to be worshipped within the cavity of Brahman.
In the first triad of the Śyāmā sandals, the three *tāras*, "kumārī vāk glauṃ," should be joined;
thereafter, the remainder is the same.

This Great Sandalwood (Mahāpādukā), which embodies the synthesis of all mantras, which reflects upon one's own identity, and which bestows great accomplishment, should be worshipped at the End of the Twelve (dvādaśānta).
Thus the garland of rays is complete;
he whose every limb consists of the body of pure knowledge is indeed Paramaśiva. (Parks 10.50)
Now, the deities of obstacles:
the first [mantra] is *irimili kirikili pada parimiro*.
The second is: *praṇava* (oṃ), *māyā* (hrīḥ), *namo bhagavati mahātripurād bhaivarṇād*, followed by the word *ravi*, then *anu mama traipurarakṣāṃ kuru kuru*.
"Saṃhara saṃhara vighnarakṣovibhīṣakān kālaya huṃ phaṭ svāhā"—this is the third.
"Blūṃ raktābhyo yoginībhyo namaḥ"—this is the fourth.
"Sāṃ sārasāya bahvāśanāya namaḥ"—this is the fifth.
"Dumuluṣu muluṣu māyā cāmuṇḍāyai namaḥ" is the sixth. These mantras are the deities that cause obstacles during the recitation of Lalitā. (Parks 10.51)

"Laughing, O goddess of speech whose words are full of laughter, having spoken the measured word, O attendants of song, perform for me the destruction of fear and obstacles—the pair [sa-visarga] and the three [tha-sounds] with the visarga"—thus is Śyāmā, the goddess who removes obstacles.
"Salutation to Staṃ, the paralyzer"—thus is Kolamukhī, the goddess who removes obstacles.
These should be recited at the commencement of each respective recitation. // Parks_10.54 //
Lalitā is in the forenoon;
Śyāmā is in the afternoon;
Vārtālī is at night.
It is supreme during the *brāhma* hour. (Parks 10.55)

Only after carefully considering the place, the time, one's own nature, one's strength, the agitation of the vital breaths, one's companions, one's illness, and one's age, should one engage in the fifth and subsequent reflections accordingly. (Parks 10.56)
Non-conflict with all living beings. (Parks 10.57)
The suppression of those who are adversaries. // Parks_10.58 //
Bestowing favor upon those who have sought refuge. // Parks_10.59 //
One's conduct toward the teacher’s son, wife, and others should be like that toward the teacher himself. (Parks 10.60)
One should personally abandon the practice of the first [type of person], as it is seen in the scriptures to be fraught with faults. (10.61)

One should partake of that food which is joyful, pleasing, fragrant, light, or derived from trees; whether it be made of molasses, flour, bark, or flowers; or whatever is prepared according to the local custom.
Immediately thereafter, one should not release the middle two fingers.
This rule does not apply to food obtained through begging.
But in the case of the middle [initiation], when one performs the act of slaying oneself, the mantra for that occasion is as follows:
"Awake, O beast! For you are not Śiva; you are indeed Śiva.
This body has been cut by Śiva; through me, may you attain the state of Śiva."
Thus [ends the verse], Parks 10.63.
In all cases, one's engagement [with speech] is preceded by verbal expression. (Parks 10.64)
There is no calamity for the ten family trees. // Parks 10.65 //

Upon seeing a grove of women, a jar, a perfected *siddha*, a bearer of the *liṅga*, a maiden crowded with play, a cluster of mango trees, an *aśoka* tree, a cemetery, a mad prostitute, one dressed in black or red garments, or an intoxicated elephant, one should perform prostration. (Parks 10.66) On the five festival days (*parvan*), there is especially meritorious worship. (Parks 10.67)
The conventional practices (*samayācāra*) extend from the stages of the beginning, fresh youth, maturity, and the end of that, up to the state of mental agitation (*unmanā*).
Beyond that, one acts according to one's desire (*yathākāmī*).
In the free conduct (*svairavyavahāra*) involving heroes (*vīra*) and non-heroes (*avīra*), there is a fall downward due to improper reflection. (Parks 10.68)
The non-abandonment of blood, the avoidance of attacking those who are detached, and the refraining from seducing those who are indifferent. // Parks_10.69 //
The gradual suppression of compassion, apprehension, fear, shame, disgust, family, caste, and character. // Parks_10.70 //

When both a guru and a *praguru* are present together, one first pays homage to the *praguru*; thereafter, out of deference to him, one refrains from bowing to the *guru* in his presence. (Parks 10.71)
Not turning one's back toward those who are worthy of honor. // Parks_10.72 //
